references.text: In Matthew's parallel account of the Sadducees' question about the resurrection, the Pharisees react to Jesus' answer. The scribes who praise Jesus in [ref:Luk 20:39|Luke 20:39] correspond to the Pharisees who gather after hearing that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees ([ref:Matt 22:34-35|Matthew 22:34-35]).

In Mark's parallel account, one of the scribes comes to Jesus after hearing the discussion and seeing that Jesus answered them well ([ref:Mark 12:28|Mark 12:28]). This confirms that the scribes recognized the quality of Jesus' answer, just as they do in [ref:Luk 20:39|Luke 20:39].

In [ref:Mark 12:32|Mark 12:32], the scribe says: "Well said, Teacher!" (Καλῶς, διδάσκαλε), which is almost identical in wording to [ref:Luk 20:39|Luke 20:39] where the scribes say: "Teacher, you have spoken well" (Διδάσκαλε, καλῶς εἶπας).

The context for the scribes' praise is Jesus' convincing answer to the Sadducees about the resurrection ([ref:Luk 20:27-38|Luke 20:27-38]). The scribes, who unlike the Sadducees believed in the resurrection, were naturally delighted that Jesus had refuted the Sadducees' objections.

Right after the scribes praise Jesus, [ref:Luk 20:40|Luke 20:40] reports that no one dared to ask him any more questions. The scribes' acknowledgment in verse 39 thus reinforces the impression that Jesus' wisdom was unquestionable.

In [ref:Apg 23:8-9|Acts 23:8-9], we see a similar pattern: the Pharisees (to whom the scribes largely belonged) defend Paul against the Sadducees and say "We find nothing wrong with this man." The conflict between the Pharisees/scribes and the Sadducees over belief in the resurrection creates a situation where the scribes support the one arguing for the resurrection.
